Chapter 8: Building Sustainable Movements and Avoiding Burnout
Let’s dive into something that’s at the heart of abolitionist organizing—making this work sustainable for the long haul, and finding ways to avoid burnout.
If you’ve ever been part of a movement, you know it’s rarely a sprint. It’s more of a marathon, filled with obstacles, setbacks, and moments where everything feels urgent.
So, how do you keep going, and how does a movement stay resilient—not just for a few months, but for years?
One big challenge is burnout. It shows up when the pressure gets heavy, resources are stretched thin, and it feels like you’re always pushing against the tide. That exhaustion and even disillusionment? It’s real, and it’s common.
Abolitionist movements know this, and that’s why they put care—both for yourself and for each other—right at the center of everything.
There are a few key strategies that really make a difference:
First, set realistic goals. Change takes time. It’s about recognizing every small win along the way and celebrating progress, even if it feels incremental.
Next, share leadership. Instead of piling everything onto one or two people, spread out the responsibility. That way, no one gets overwhelmed, and everyone feels invested.
Build supportive relationships. Imagine a network where you can ask for help, offer support, and know you’re not alone. That sense of community makes all the difference.
And don’t forget to prioritize rest and renewal. Taking breaks, reflecting on the work, or just spending time on something that recharges you—it’s not a luxury. It’s essential.
What does this look like in real life? It might mean starting every meeting with a quick check-in, making decisions together as a group, or even setting aside time for a retreat focused on healing and connection.
Some groups go a step further, creating dedicated “care teams” to support members through tough times or transitions. It’s about having each other’s backs, no matter what.
Sustainability also means being honest about what you can and can’t do. It’s better to focus on a few things and do them well, instead of spreading yourself too thin and risking burnout.
The movements that last? They’re the ones that adapt, learn from their mistakes, and make room for joy and celebration—no matter how tough things get.
So, here’s the key takeaway: When you center care and sustainability, you’re not just protecting yourself and your community—you’re making sure the work can keep moving forward, even when setbacks come your way.
